utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We notice that Mr. Naletilic is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour. We were -- have not been told the reason. I suppose he's not feeling well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Madam court deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I received a phone call from the detention centre and he will be resting this afternoon. He's sending a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll proceed without Mr. Naletilic's presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours, because I have the general authorisation of my client that we can always proceed even in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please? [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd forgotten to switch my microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zoric, just a brief comment before we begin, to make it easier for to us follow one another, and the -- and so that the interpreters can follow it and that we'll also help the Chamber and our learned friends, also enable everybody to follow you, we shall both therefore endeavour to try as slow as possible, yet not too slow so as not to slow down the pace of the proceedings, but -- and to help you with this, I do not know whether you can see on the monitor the transcript, as I'm talking?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Well, then, you can look at this black dot at the end and when it stops it means I have finished and you can start your answer. Will that be all right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, to start with, will you please introduce yourself, give us your brief facts from your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I'm Damir Zoric, I was born on the 1st of January, 1960, in Grude, Bosnia-Herzegovina. My family migrated to Zagreb when I was still a boy and ever since I've been living in Zagreb. I'm married, a father of two, all my education was in Zagreb. The elementary, the secondary, the faculty of philosophy in Zagreb and that is where I also obtained my Ph.D. Degree. I studied -- I read history and ethnology, that is roughly the equivalent much cultural anthropology in western terms. I also worked at the same department as a scientific worker and performing different duties, and as -- from 1991, I worked in the government of the Republic of Croatia, first as an adviser to the deputy Prime Minister for humanitarian affairs, that is the time when the government of national unit, and that was August, 1991, was formed in Zagreb. And then pursuant to the order of the same government, I founded and was the main secretary of the government office for expelled persons and refugees, and I did that until about April, 1993. I was then elected to parliament in the first elections for the counties Chamber of the diet of Croatia. It was roughly the senate in a two-Chamber diet, and as the leader, or head of the parliamentary opposition, I was elected as one of deputy speakers of that Chamber. From the -- from late 1995, I once again went back to work with refugees and expelled persons, and I first became the deputy and then the head of that office. I held that position for slightly less than two years. After that, I was appointed by the government, the director of the state pensioners' fund. In February, rather in January, 1999, I was appointed the ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and I held that office until the 1st of November, 2000. After that, I went back to Zagreb. And now I work for a private company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: During your term as a MP, which party did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At that time I was a member of the leading opposition party, which in 1991, and for a part of 1992, made part of the government of national unity together with all the other parties but at the time when I was elected, it led the opposition in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during your time as a MP, because these are the years of -- that we are concerned with, was there any decision passed by the diet in relation to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I do not know if the diet ever took any operative decisions. Decisions that were taken there were always decisions either hearing reports and adoption of reports as to the relations between the two states, things that were done, different procedures taking place between the two states. In other words, all the chief decisions on the recognition and all the rest had already been adopted before I became a MP. I do not know which specific decision you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I don't have in mind any specific decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Maybe it's a technical error but I cannot find the transcript to which party did Mr. Zoric belong, opposition party but what was the name of the party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, maybe you could clarify it for us, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It was called the Croatian Social Liberal Party, and it is -- it was the first party that was founded in Croatia in 1989. And I was one -- I was among its founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When I asked you about diet decisions I didn't mean any specific decision. What I had in mind was in view of the very close relations between the two states, did any decision or perhaps a discussion preceding such a decision reflect mutual respect or disrespect?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: All discussions, agreements, decisions, all -- everything that went on in the Croatian diet had to do with agreement between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. All these decisions are public, they were all published by the Official Gazette. I do not think that there is a single decision, such as the one you mentioned, that would belittle the other or that would show disrespect to the other state. No, they all pursued the regulation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the B and H. That is to one state with another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there some bipartite agreements that would be the subject of debate in the diet concerning any salient issues between the two states, borders, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Republic of Croatia has the largest number of signed bilateral, that is interstate agreement with Bosnia-Herzegovina. With no other state have we ever had so many agreements. At different stages, after their conclusion, after their ratification, they have been ratified. Others have not. Some of them have been ratified by one side, not by the other. But with that country, we have the largest possible number of agreements. The Republic of Croatia has signed agreement on borders with the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that agreement was signed at a meeting of the stability pact in 1999, in early August, 1999, and that is the only border agreement which two states emerged from the former Yugoslavia ever signed. There are no two other states which have succeeded in resolving that matter. And Croatian has done it with Bosnia-Herzegovina, after very major effort, after a lot of effort invested and that agreement was signed by presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, the diet adopted the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. What do you know about the diet at that time? If you know, were there any -- did the -- did Croatia undertake any obligations, any responsibility, towards the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The constitution in one of its articles, and I believe it is the tenth, I'm not quite sure, but I think it was the tenth article which stipulated that the Republic of Croatia was bound to take certain care about Croats outside the Republic of Croatia, which also of course included the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they are outside the Republic of Croatia but that also relates to the Croats living in Voyvodina and in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, do you know anything about some, as I call them, transcripts of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, this was quite a topic in the media. I know what the majority of people with an average knowledge in Croatia, with all the controversies and all the controversies that accompanied the story about transcripts so that I can say -- I can talk about them only on the basis only of what I learned from the media or things that I know from the area of legislation, that is how such issues should be treated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And will you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: This matter is regulated by a special act, I do not know what it is called. It's something about the protection of archival documentation or something. I'm not quite sure what this is called but there are some other regulations on that that is the state secret, the classification of information, so there is a procedure which I think makes part of some normal, regular state norm, states how one treats such matters. As far as I know, the current government, after all that happened in that regard, decided to place these documents under seal, under protection, for the next 20 or 30 years, and said that it should be treated as prescribed by the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know why such a decision following the discussions in the diet?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, I know some of the reasons, either from media or from some private contacts with my colleagues who are still in the diet, and are still members of individual parliamentary boards. And who suggested such discussion and decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour maybe the witness will just clarify the period of time, when the legislation was adopted, because Croatia is a new state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seric, would you please ask this question to the witness so that it will clarify this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Seric, do you or Mr. Krsnik intend to call a witness who will actually tell us the date and the name of the various acts that have been referred to and show us the act? Because this witness is, as you know, giving his information based on what he has acquired from the media, which is not always the most reliable source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour, you know that we've always avoided the media but we shall be tendering these laws through our next witness, and this gentleman here was a MP so there were parliamentary boards which discussed these matters. We only have to wait a little, and then you will hear why all that happened, and the most important thing, Your Honour, is what the defence has been claiming from day one, and that is that the transcripts that we see here have got here illegally and so on and so forth, I don't want to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Has very fairly said that he doesn't really know, he knows of but he doesn't know precisely, so if you're going to call another witness, we don't have to push this witness so hard on his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take your liberty, Your Honour, with all due respect but this gentleman personally knows about that from the parliamentary boards which discussed it, and their decision was very important. We just have to it wait a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: He said himself, Mr. Krsnik, and Mr. Seric, on a number of occasions, that the media is his sole source of information. That's the only reason why I had hoped there would be somebody who would be able to quote chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, let us round this off. Do you have any personal knowledge about the presidential transcripts, their fate, or is it only second hand information from what you heard or read?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. When I said that I did not know exactly, it's simply that I really wouldn't be able to quote the name of the law because laws are usually have very long and intricate names but it is called roughly law on the protection of archival documents and other -- and I think it relates to the confidentiality, state secret and so on and so forth. I mean these laws have very long titles. That is it. But I know roughly what it's called and where I could find it. I mean this law does exist, and people who are directly involved in this matters can show you. But regardless of what the media wrote or did not write, this was a matter which was of a paramount political importance at a certain point in time. And people that I talked with and who are my close friends and who hold high offices in the diet, in the national security board and other boards, they insisted on the respect, on the compliance with the law, and I think that made the government adopt some operative decisions to store, to keep this documentation in conformity with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us when that legislation was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After its recognition, Croatia pursued a very intensive legislative activity and these laws were adopted during the previous government. When exactly, if I -- I find it difficult to say but it must have been seven perhaps or more years ago, before they became the chief topic in the media and political life and these laws have not suffered any changes, they are still in force. That is, they are not laws which were taken by the new parliamentary majority but the earlier one. And that of course also goes for most other laws in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you were an active participant, being a MP, in the work of the supreme legislative body, can you tell the Chamber what was the diet's policy with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina and what were its manifestations and I mean the time -- I mean your term, that is 1992, 1993? Let us focus on that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I was elected to the diet in 1993. The diet, in conformity with its procedure and laws and the constitution, of course, which governed its work, the diet adopted all sorts of declarations, conclusions, decisions, which were then addressed to the government. All the discussions pursued -- and sometimes they took a very long time, but we all pursued consensus on those important issues, because the awareness prevailed regardless on what side of the diet I sat on, that these are matters of paramount importance, and the -- and the MPs tried to bring, to coordinate, and to arrive at unanimous decisions so that -- and they did always, so that whenever it came to matters relative to Bosnia-Herzegovina, such decisions, such conclusions were usually after these long debates passed unanimously. And when there were certain disagreements during the war, or regarding the situation in one or the other country, then it was always said that they needed to be solved in agreement with the international community, with the mediation of the international community, and so that the -- all constituent peoples in the B and H, that is what the constitution of that country said, and their former constitutions as well, that is the Serbs, Muslims, Bosniaks and Croats, that their mutual relations should be solved in an equal and mutually acceptable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You were then the representative of the strongest opposition party in the diet. Can you tell us, but very briefly, very briefly indeed, something -- the relations between the HDZ of Croatia and HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that was frequently raised here and the attitude of the HDZ as the party in government to the parliamentary decisions?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time they had the majority, and like every party that has the majority they had the opportunity to pass the decisions on their own, but in a number of cases that were of particular importance, attempts were always made to reach a consensus. They didn't take our views into account on all occasions but in the majority of cases, particularly cases of this nature that we are now talking about, they did, and most of the conclusions were reached by consensus. I can't remember now any decisions or conclusions that were imposed or pushed through by the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, you say that you were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution claims that the purpose of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was to create close ties with the Republic of Croatia and that the Republic of Croatia let it be known that they support the efforts and the endeavours of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can you tell us whether there were any discussions in the diet, in this sense, in the going in the direction of any kind of recognition of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the acceptance of this territory, this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No. We knew very well where the borders were between the two states. We knew very well what the Republic of Croatia was and what Bosnia and Herzegovina was. We distinguished between the two. And as for the cooperation and the close ties, I think that it's quite natural, because it's quite natural all over the world, because cross-boundary cooperation is something that everybody strives for. As for the actual recognition, this was not even discussed at all. It was not mentioned. I'm not aware of any official paper accepted or adopted by the parliament or the diet where any form of internal organisation or structure within Bosnia and Herzegovina, including those by Croats, where such structures would be mentioned. We always spoke about the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we spoke about the peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they were the categories in the constitution, Croats, Bosniaks or Muslims, because that was the term used at the time, and Serbs. And about the need for them to come to solution that would be satisfactory to all sides that would be reached by negotiations. The international community engaged in similar efforts at the same time. All the international mediators that were active, either in Croatia or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or in both states at the same time, they did the same. From Mr. Vance, who was the special envoy for a time, then Mr. Herbert Ochem [phoen] And then Cutilheiro, Vance-Owen, Stoltenberg and all the others. In 1991 and 1992, I had the opportunity to take part in such meetings, because I was a member of the first governmental commission for the cooperation with UNPROFOR at the time when General Satish Nambiar was the force commander, and I am really quite familiar with the general orientation of the general kind of advice that the international mediators gave us, the general thrust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you are eager to give your testimony, but if the Defence counsel need more information, he will ask follow-up questions. Let's concentrate on the questions asked by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Also, can I ask you, Mr. Zoric, when exactly in 1993 did you become a member of the opposition party in government? Which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not become a member of the opposition party in 1993. That was in 1989 that I joined that party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, when did you become an elected member of parliament. That's what I'm talking about. You said it was 1993. When in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In spring. I think it was in April. That's when the elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, we will now come to an area that you actually dealt with, the operation of your office for the expelled persons and refugees. Can you please tell us what happened in light of the huge number of expelled persons and refugees? How did the Republic of Croatia and its institutions treat the refugees and the expelled persons, first from the Republic of Croatia and then we will deal more specifically with the problem of such persons coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe my learned colleague will split somehow the questions because it's a very, very long and complicated question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It will it be very difficult to follow the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that, and I also advise the Defence counsel to concentrate on the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. That's what I intended but I wanted to start from the very beginning of the operation of the office, it to see whether there was any difference in the treatment. That's why I wanted to lay the foundation for my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, let's start from the establishment of the office for the expelled persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, there was a rather small service that was part of the ministry for social welfare, that was to deal with or take care of the expelled persons after the beginning of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia. However, in summer, 1991, already, the number of such persons was so great, and it grew so rapidly, that it became quite clear that a specialised service should be established as soon as possible. We did not have any such services before. We didn't have any experience or any knowledge as to how this job should be done, nor did we expect that anything of that magnitude would happen. So in autumn, 1991, we started the preparations for the establishment of a specialised office which would be a part of the government, and I was asked to help establish it and organise it, and I accepted the job. What we did was we took the social welfare offices, which existed in every municipality and which dealt with social welfare issues, we instructed them to concentrate and to devote most of their attention to the expelled persons and refugees from the Republic of Croatia, and then we organised several of such municipal offices into regional offices, depending on the actual concentration of the refugees and expelled persons, where their numbers were greater. There were some 20 such regional offices and they did not fully correspond to the territorial structure of the Republic of Croatia, which is divided into counties. They were organised on the functional principle, not territorial, where there was a greater number of persons that had to be taken care of we had a regional office to do that there. In 1992, Croatia had about 250.000 internally displaced persons so that after the occupation of, capture of Vukovar, in one night only, more than 20.000 people arrived in Zagreb. Since it was already winter time, that was in late November, we found accommodation for them in hotels. And later, we tried to find accommodation for them to the social welfare premises or buildings. That was quite difficult because there is a slight difference between, let's call it a council flat and the Hotel Intercontinental. In March, in spring 1992, we already had about 20.000 refugees who had come from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at that time, we already had the office of the UNHCR, the UN high commissioner for refugees. Later on, there was also the international organisation for migrations and virtually every humanitarian organisation had its office. And we tried to coordinate our assistance with their assistance. Croatia had already adopted some regulations regarding the rights of the displaced persons and refugees, because there is a certain difference in the international law between a person having the status of refugee and a person having the status of the displaced person. The UNHCR advised us in this respect because as I have already said, we did not have any experience with this kind of thing. We cooperated very well with the UNHCR. I gave them my office to their disposal, and we actually worked in the same building for a while. And then sometime in 1993, when the entire -- when the whole crisis escalated due to the intensification of their operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had to seek new premises, larger premises, but at first we worked in the same building, and then the IOM, the international organisation for migrations, used the same building where we were. In March, 1992, Croatia had about 20.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the areas where Bosnian Serbs had set up their autonomous regions, as they called it, and these were the areas where they expelled all the non-Serb inhabitants, that is Muslims and Croats. The ratio is -- was at the time about 70 per cent of Muslims and about 30 per cent of Croats, because that was the ethnic composition of the population in the areas such as Prijedor, Bosanska Dubica and some other areas in north-western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I think your answer is too long, and the Defence counsel will guide you question by question and step by step. We will come to that point. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, but since the witness probably senses where my questions are going, he now, in effect, answered ten of the questions that I wanted to ask him. And thereby he speeded up the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how did the Republic of Croatia, and your office, treat the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina? Where was accommodation found for them? Was there any difference in the way that they were treated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At first, they were housed in the buildings where the displaced persons from Croatia were already housed. But in the spring of 1992, we had already -- we already had no free accommodation left, and the number of people coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina rose rapidly. As I already said n March, we had slightly less than 20.000 refugees and only a month later, we had 200.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that in just one month, almost 180.000 people came to Croatia, and then in August, the figure rose to 370.000 refugees. This information is completely the same as the information that can be obtained from the international organisations, and in such conditions, it became very hard to provide appropriate accommodation for all of them. And then we started building several settlements or project -- housing projects in Croatia, several of them, with the assistance of the international community and in coordination with the UNHCR. But according to the law, they all had the same kind of treatment and they all had the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, we heard some witnesses say that their accommodation in, for instance, on the island of Obonjan, they described it almost as a camp of some sort. What is your knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Objection. I have never heard any witness here in the courtroom talking about Obonjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that refugee centre in that island was mentioned in the direct examinations, in the Prosecution's case, but I don't remember whether it is described as a camp of some sort. And Mr. Seric, maybe you could ask a general question to this witness about the situations in that refugee centre on that island?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly what I will do. It's really simpler that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what was the accommodation like and in particular what was the accommodation like on the island of Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I can describe it for you, but I agree with all those who say that being a refugee is not something nice. It is a very difficult position to find yourself in. These are the people who have been expelled and because of some great tragedy or suffering or fear, they had to find refuge somewhere else. I heard people say that we organised -- that we set up a camp but this is something that really makes no sense because there is a very big difference between a person coming to a place of his own free will, seeking refuge, and on the other hand a person who is brought somewhere by force. And forced to go there. We were not happy that these people had come and that we had to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the time frame, when? Which is the period of time the witness is talking about? 1992, 1993 or maybe afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric, you may ask some questions specifying the time frame for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness did specify it a few questions ago, he said -- he specified the exact time when about 370.000 refugees had come to Croatia from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he said that it was in 1993 in April?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in 1992 already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this figure was valid for 1993. But he can repeat it. Please do, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In spring of 1992, in March, 1992, we had slightly less than 20.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the areas where the Bosnian Serbs had expelled people because they organised their SAO Krajinas there, the Serbian autonomous regions of Krajina. And only a month later, the figure rose to 200.000 people. And by August, the figure was 370.000 people. This figure shows the -- how fast their number rose, and I think that it also corresponds to the period when the military operations in that area intensified, as the weather got better the war got worse and escalated. We who had to deal with this, who had to take care of about 300.000 people who were internally displaced in the Republic of Croatia, this put us in a very difficult situation where we had to do the impossible. All the more so because at the beginning, we did not have any international assistance in this regard. The representatives of the international communities, I do not want to belittle their contribution, but I think that I'm telling the truth if I say that at first they came in small delegations and they saw the way the situation was, and they merely reported to their headquarters, and these people had to be housed, they had to be fed, they had to receive medical treatment, their children had to it attend school. And this entire logistics had to be organised. We would not have been able to do so had we not had the great solidarity of the population, the population showed great solidarity. The entire areas close to the border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour it seems to me that we are getting too far away from the Obonjan island.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. If you have any further questions concerning of the Obonjan island, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a slightly different temperament from Mr. Krsnik, but Mr. Prosecutor asked the witness to go back and to go through his whole testimony right from the beginning, and now he is dictating to me, he is telling me how to conduct my examination and to go straight back to Obonjan. I think he may be right, but at any rate, he wanted to intervene when I wanted to ask a question about Obonjan, he wanted to hear about the time frame, but at any rate, can you please tell us what were the housing conditions at the -- on the island of Obonjan? What were the transportation links from the island to the main land? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It is not a large island. It is located near Sibenik, off the coast near Sibenik. There was a boy scouts camp there. I think it was an international camp because it was called the seventh continent. There were some buildings where we could house these people. There was an outpatient clinic, there was the kitchen. And there were also some buildings where people could be housed, at least in the summer. There was a -- even a theatre, and other things that are necessary for social life. There was even a swimming pool. But as soon as the people were housed there, we immediately started building permanent housing so that, as early as in autumn, the permanent solid housing existed on the island. We did it in cooperation with the German government. And the people from the doctors without borders, it's a French organisation of physicians, and some other organisations that I cannot recall at this moment, they worked together with us, right from the beginning. And the representatives from the UNHCR also went there. At first, because of the war which was being waged in Sibenik at the time in 1991, the local transportation services were abandoned. They no longer existed. But however, we insisted that boat line be re-established. And this service exists to this day. And at our request, the service was established. The vessel was not large. It could accommodate perhaps 50 to 60 people but that's the same boat that connects the main land with all the other islands in this area. So you could not put 1.000 people on a boat and make it possible for them to go to the mainland to the town, and to see a movie. Perhaps 30 of them could go. But they were not tourists, they were refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, was there a decree or a law regulating the rights of the refugees? And was it valid for everybody in a systematic manner?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At first there was a decree that was passed by the government and it was used as the foundation for the law regulating this very issue. The legal advisers of the international organisations, primarily the UNHCR, helped us to harmonise the terminology and the standards with the international standards when drafting this law, and this law was passed even before the escalation of the refugee crisis. I mean the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The law regulated the rights of the refugees and displaced persons to care in the same way. The only difference is that in legal terms, there was a difference or a distinction between the displaced persons, internally displaced persons, and the refugees, persons who had come from another state. There were refugees from Serbia, from Kosovo, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and regardless of the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina that they came from, they were always treated as refugees. But the rights that they enjoyed were the same as the rights of the Croatian citizens who had been expelled from the occupied areas. They were entitled to accommodation, food, education primary medical care, and in cases of life and death, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, where did the funds come from?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The only reliable source of funds was the Croatian budget, and about 85 per cent of the needed funds came from the budget, and about 15 per cent came from international sources, that is donations and the international organisations. Donations were something that came from time to time and were of a rather limited scope, and these people had to live every day, and care for them of course cost every day. The biggest shock for me personally, when I did that, came sometime in early 1992 when we had to organise funerals for some of these people, because there were also people who died as refugees, especially if they were old or sick. And there was no humanitarian organisation which would assume upon itself to cover those costs. In Zagreb most of these people were put up and it was about 15 per cent of the Zagreb population, and in Zagreb, as in every large city, funeral is a very costly matter. Now, the question arises where to find cemeteries for these people? The question arises of respecting their religious beliefs and traditions. Hardly any one of them would agree to cremation because they all somehow lived confident that they would eventually be buried back in their local cemeteries. But it was all very expensive and in such -- under such circumstances, the only reliable source of funds is the budget. As far as I know, the Republic of Croatia spent about 1.6 billion dollars, American dollars, for these particular purposes. Of that, about half a billion for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, did Croatia send humanitarian aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina, both for Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally did that. Not only for humanitarian but also for practical reasons, because we knew that it was better to support those people so that they could stay in their own country rather than come to us and be dependent on our care, especially since we were fast learners and understood that there was also a war in human beings. After shelling, they would also send you usually 15 or 20.000 people so as to produce chaos in the rear. And it was not easy to help all those people and that is why we thought it was much better to help them in places where they already lived. Of course the other reason for that was the humanitarian one. We were witness to the great relief and understanding that people from other countries showed towards us and we thought that we should also help the needy in our turn, and I personally took some convoys into some parts of BH, not only to those populated by Croats but also to those inhabited by Muslims, and after all, if you are moving through mixed areas, taking food along, then it is only logical that all sides will expect you to help them, and we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, can you tell us and especially Their Honours something about the registration of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia and in particular with regard to men of military age?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: A person who would find himself or herself in our territory would apply to the nearest office to be registered, and then would be issued papers, identity papers showing their status. We could not differentiate between able-bodied men of military men, of non-able bodied, because the law and a realistic fear of war to also be a reason for the recognition of the status. That is what the international conventions stipulate. But representatives of the Muslim side in Sarajevo, in the course of talks in Zagreb, and that included Mr. Izetbegovic, regularly demanded from us not to receive -- not to grant the refugee status to any able-bodied men. And then there would be some -- then media or religious representatives or somehow else, they invited them to join the struggle for the freedom of their country, but we, our office, could not deny them this status and we did not do that. And after all, one can see it from the rosters of these people, because these were not only women and children, there were also men, that is families as often as not, and we often worked to bring families together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know in your offices work and your personal work, were there any members of the BH Army in Croatia who were either refugees or receiving treatment after wounding?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such. My office had a large warehouse at the Zagreb fair grounds, and an adjacent pavilion, or rather an adjacent hall, served as a warehouse for -- as Bosnian Muslim logistics warehouse. And it involved civilians and their highest religious representatives in Croatia and in Sarajevo. They were collecting everything from food on. But we were also aware that there were other things there. And as for the treatment? The -- an overwhelming majority of the members of the Bosnian army was treated in Sarajevo, no, excuse me, in Split, because that would be natural point of destination as the only point of entry into or exit from Bosnia was towards the Croatian coast. On the other hand, throughout the siege of Bihac, and it was under siege for several years, all the logistics came from Zagreb. That is from the Zagreb airport. Helicopters took off every day to take into that area all the basic necessities for these people and there were about 50.000 people in that enclave under siege. So you can imagine the logistics bridge, this air lift, which was provided supplying them with both weapons and food and fuel and all the rest they needed to survive for almost three years of an encirclement, and I know that several helicopters of that kind unfortunately were brought down and with tragic consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the time frame for this last thing?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, this went on all the time, between 1995 -- until the liberation, until the Croatian Army joined forces with the federation army, on the Croatian-Bosnian border near Plitvice, that is until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, can you tell us, but in a sentence or two, the structure of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina? Can you give us a couple of figures, some statistics, if you please?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, the largest number of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina were Muslims, Bosniaks, about 70 per cent of them, and a little less, about 30 per cent, were Croats. And a small, small -- and the others, including some Serbs, accounted for the rest, but a very small percentage. Later on, the number of Muslims -- the share of Muslims dropped but the overall number increased, so that it was about half-half, 50-50. One half came from the areas which are more or less the Serb entities of BH and the other half came from the areas which today roughly, more or less, represent the federation that is the Croat-Bosniak entity. From 1993, and especially from 1994 onward, when some front lines had already stabilised, some people returned to BH, but most of them had already gone to other countries, mostly to third countries, mostly West European countries, because those countries took in certain quotas of people. And in view of a large number of migrants from the former country, who had been living -- who have already been living in western Europe, many of them just took in other relations so that after three or four months in Croatia, those refugees usually went on, as a rule to Germany but also to other countries, the Netherlands, Norway, a little less to other countries. And I assumed, that is one of the reasons why people on Obonjan felt a little isolated. Let me go back to that because it wasn't so easy for them perhaps to communicate with representatives of international organisations as those who were in Zagreb, say, or in Split. And that was why we asked the UNHCR, and it was on that, to send a representative and they also opened a small office there. Apart from that, if I may, and I wish to mention this, after this facility was vacated, that is when the war ended and when the refugees left, this island -- I mean all the accommodation facilities there have been converted to a foreign languages centre and I gave you a publication which shows what kind of activities are pursued there today, and these are all the facilities that once accommodated refugees. This document, this publication, I was given by my son who brought it from his school, and he will also go there this summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will tender it later on. I believe this is now time for the break, Mr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's time for the break. Since we have only one accused this afternoon, we will have 20 minutes' break. We will resume at ten to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the witness, please? Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three? Is it better?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. It seems there was some problem with the interpretation. Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, you told us about accommodation conditions. Now, can you tell us what do you know about the quantity, quality and the manner of food preparation for refugees, in particular preparation of food for Muslim Bosniaks, refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: When the crisis escalated in a month, in some facilities they became a majority. And then some of them began to request that food be prepared for them in a different way, in conformity with their customs. And they also had, of course, their hygienic habits were different, and we of course had to respect that whenever we could. And that is how we began to open new facilities to put the Bosniak refugees. They themselves opened some of these facilities through their organisations, their mother country, cooperatives, Merhamet, their charity organisation, and we then took in those we could. Some of these facilities did not meet even the basic, the minimum, standards of hygiene so that we closed them down and accommodated refugees elsewhere, so that some of these facilities which sprang up practically overnight in some parts of Zagreb, we moved those refugees to Varazdin for instance, where we refurbished a barracks or rather two large barracks for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, did religious -- were religious communities active among the refugees? And did they provide religious services for Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of such organisations, international organisations, was Igasa this is an international Islamic -- international organisations. There were others too but this was one of the bigger ones, and Merhamet also did that. And in many facilities, they had their makeshift praying facilities, or we would set aside a building for that, and they also had their own schools with curricula of their choice. And whenever possible, we endeavoured to integrate school children in the regular schooling system of our country, so that all refugee children, that is I do not know of any case, of any child, not being in school. All the children regularly attended school in the Republic of Croatia so that in Zagreb and a number of larger places, we had classes which were almost twice as required by the educational standards. We simply filled the class rooms to capacity. But all the children were incorporated, all the children had education provided for them, and in those places where the teachers were refugees themselves, we helped them start their own supplementary classes or schools where they could instruct children in those specific particular subjects which could not be provided, which could not be taught by our teachers. There were several such schools, and to all intents and purposes in every refugee centre you could find such a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let us now focus on the period of the conflict between the BH Army and the Croat Defence Council in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was the -- how did the institutions of the Republic of Croatia, and your office, treat Bosniaks, Muslims, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Our attitude did not change, during some periods of time, perhaps there were some additional psychological burden, and that would apply particularly to refugees, but basically, the -- our attitude did not change. They were received in Croatia throughout, and they were taken care of in an identical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was their attitude towards institutions, the office and the other institutions of the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there were some quite funny situations, where the refugees somehow supported one side or the other because there were members of various ethnic communities involved in the conflict housed in the same location. Sometimes these -- this caused tensions among them and we sometimes had situations when husbands who would come to visit their families during the weekend would spend time in the same housing facility and then they would go back to their original homes and continue to fight each other. Sometimes we had some offending or derogatory attitude but that's life. We tried to provide the same level of care in accordance with our legal and humane obligations. We never had any objections lodged by any major international organisations protesting against any violations of the refugee rights. Quite the contrary. We always received commendations from the international organisations saying we really did our job well. And the international communities at the time that dealt with this issue were mostly staffed by the people who had experience from various other crises in Asia, South America, Africa and so on so perhaps they were really able to make a comparison with our situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What do you know about the political activities of the refugees, Bosniak Muslims in Croatia? Were they able to participate in any parties or any other organisations? Were they able to take part in the elections?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time period, Zagreb was in fact more of the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina than Sarajevo itself, because Sarajevo was isolated and Zagreb was not. So their entire communications with the world went through Zagreb. Various representatives were located there, and they had the full freedom of activity, be it humanitarian activity, political activity, whatever they needed at any given point in time. And they were able to conduct these activities through Zagreb. The entire supply system went through Croatia. All the people got in and got out through Croatia. There was a single bridge, to be more specific the only bridge that linked the south and north. It was half torn down but all the traffic went through that bridge across that bridge, and the traffic was never halted. As for the political activities, in 1996, the first post-war elections were held in Bosnia and Herzegovina under the auspices of the OSCE, and one of the countries where the voting took place outside of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, among the people who had left the country, was Croatia. I was in charge of that operation. About 120.000 people registered to vote, and in accordance with the rules that were put in place by the OSCE, politicians from various political parties were able to visit places where refugees, a larger number of refugees were. Croats or Muslims. Trying to persuade them to vote for them. And about 120.000 people took part in the elections. There were three major political options that were presented to those people in Croatia. The political parties of the -- the political party of the Croats in BiH, that is the HDZ, and they visited areas where there were major concentrations of Croats. As for the Muslims, there was the SDA party and the party led by Mr. Abdic, the party that represented mostly people from the Cazin area. And they indeed got most of the votes in the elections. So they were able to conduct this type of activity. And at the end of the elections, our government received the commendation and the expression of gratitude from the then presiding or president of the OSCE, ambassador Falk [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, do you know anything through your activities and the activities of your office about the equipping and arming of the BH Army members? I am talking about the period 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that they had some training centres in Croatia. Practically the first weapons they got they got the weapons from Croatia. All of their logistics, all the aid that they received, including the weapons, reached them through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Zoric, in light of your introductory statement when you introduced yourself to us, I would like to know something about the issue of dual citizenship for Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: According to the Croatian constitution, every Croat regardless of where he or she lives is entitled to the Croatian citizenship. My brother lives in America. He is a Croat citizen. And at the same time an American citizen. Likewise, the Croats who do not have permanent residence in Croatia, including those in Bosnia and Herzegovina, who are citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, have the right to apply for the Croatian citizenship and are usually given it. And there is also another possibility. Croat citizens can also apply for the BH citizenship. I am a Croatian citizen, a citizen of the Republic of Croatia and when my term of office ended in Bosnia-Herzegovina, since I was born in that country, I was entitled to apply for B H citizenship, and I did get that citizenship so now I also have dual citizenship. I'm from Croatia and I have BH citizenship and most of the Croats who live in BiH have Croat citizenship too. That doesn't, however, apply only to Croats. I also know that large number of Bosniaks and even Serbs from Banja Luka applied for and got Croatian citizenship. And during my office, terms of office as an ambassador, I often had to intervene in cases involving the application for our citizenship for the family members of certain eminent persons from Sarajevo or Banja Luka. And a substantial number of well-known public figures applied for and got Croatian citizenship and they are able to travel all over the world with their Croatian passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know, since you were born there and in light of the issue of dual citizenship, were there any volunteers from Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially from Herzegovina, in the Croatian Army in the course of the aggression of the Serbs and the JNA against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few people, many people, who organised themselves because Croatia at that time did not have an organised structure to deal with it, who simply came en masse to various theatres of war in Croatia, to Vukovar and also in the Dubrovnik theatre and to the Zadar theatre, for instance. As time went by, and in light of the historical developments, a large number of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina emigrated to Croatia. My family is one of such families. And in accordance -- according to the 1991 census in Croatia, about 492.000 inhabitants -- Croatian inhabitants had originally come from Bosnia and Herzegovina, were of BH origin. And the war brought so many other people to Croatia. So the links were already close in the former state, in the former Yugoslavia. The peoples were integrated. They were in a way always going towards the centres of their own republics. So it was quite logical for people from the Croatian areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina to study in Zagreb or in Split and not in Sarajevo. And also some Serbs from Croatia, in fact the majority of them preferred to study in Belgrade than in Zagreb. It was some kind of an integration. People were trying to get integrated into the life of their own people, nation, not of their own republic. So there was this strong sense of belonging to one people, to a single people. And then when the aggression began, people really came en masse to defend the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them after the Serbian side and the JNA attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: When UNPROFOR came to Croatia, after the signing of the Sarajevo declaration, I think it was on the 3rd of January, 1992, these theatres of war stabilised more or less so that by March, by the spring, the war had already moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the substantial number of these people went back. You have to bear in mind that these people -- that the entire families lived on various addresses. Would you live in Bosnia and Herzegovina, your brother would be in Zagreb or in Split so one and the same family, members of one and the same family lived in two states. So it was quite logical for people to go back and to defend the areas where they were from. As a lay person in military terms it was quite ridiculous for me to -- when I heard people insist on going to fight as volunteers to their own village because they felt that they would be able to protect their village and prevent the village from being taken. They didn't have any military knowledge. And they failed to see that there were various methods of capturing territory. But at the beginning there was this strong sense that everybody should go back to their own villages and defend their own area. So they all went back and a large number of them went back, and defended their homeland. As for myself, it would be quite hard for me to define where my homeland is. I've lived in Zagreb for almost 30 years. But Bosnia and Herzegovina is also my homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric you were the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. In which period was that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I was the ambassador from February 1999 until November 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you were the ambassador representing the interests of the Republic of Croatia there, what was the state structure that you found in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, it was rather strange, but it wasn't something that we could do anything about. It was a state composed of two entities. One of the entities is very much centralised and has all the state attributes, has all the instances, the parliament, the President of the republic, the vice-president. Its own customs, the military. So it has all the instruments that a state needs to have. It's highly centralised. And it belonged to only one people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's the Republika Srpska. And the return of the refugees to this area went quite slow, and until this day, there hasn't been much progress made in this respect. A large number of people has been unable to return. So it's a centralised structure called the entity. Its name is the Republika Srpska on the one hand. And on the other hand there is an entity that belongs to it two peoples, Bosniaks and Muslims, Bosniaks and Croats. That's how it was defined. It is very decentralised. It's comprises ten or so cantons. Some of them are mononational, belong to only one people, and some cantons belong to both peoples and they had special administrative arrangements. They also had their own judiciary. Its own government, its own military, which has two components. The Federation armed forces consisted of the BH Army as the Bosniak component, and the Croatian Defence Council as the Croatian component. Now they are in the joints armed forces of the Federation so that when you take all that together, it was a rather unusual state structure. At the same time, the state had the high representative of the international community who in effect run -- ran the country, and the closest parallel in the history of states would be a monarch an enlightened absolutist monarch who was able to suspend the decisions of the parliament, of the government, to remove from the office members of the Presidency, which the Presidency I mean had the representatives of the three peoples, two elected from one entity and one from the other entity. So it was a very strange structure. It is the country that has the largest number of ministers in the world. I think that they had at that time about 160 ministers because every canton had its own government. It was a structure that has not been recorded in modern history of statehood. So it was a country that -- where everybody wanted that state to -- that situation to change. But the problem was that the three different sides used the same terms that had entirely different meanings for them. When a Bosniak says "Sarajevo" he means his capital and all that such a town would symbolise, but for Serbs, that meant something entirely different, when they say "capital" that's Banja Luka. Sarajevo can be a large city that is an administrative centre. For Croats, the term "capital" would mean something entirely different. So when a Bosniak says "Bosnia and Herzegovina," he or she, they do not mean the same thing that Croats do when they say "Bosnia and Herzegovina" or when Serbs say the same word. So the same terms had very, very different meanings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, when you took on the office of the ambassador, who did you give your credentials to in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At that time, I gave my credentials to the member of the Presidency, Jelavic who stood in for the Serbian member of the Presidency, Mr. Radisic, who for some reason was absent from Sarajevo. I don't know what the reason was. But at any rate, the three members, all three members of the Presidency had equal rights and they could stand in for each other. As the ambassador to Croatia, of course I got my approval from that country and it was signed by all three members of the Presidency, Croat, Serb and Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, those questions are very interesting, and we know the present situation in that country, but I wonder whether it's related to this case. Ask some more concentrated questions which are directly related to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I only have three more questions, so I will be concluding my examination quite soon any way. I think key could perhaps shed some light in retrospect to the relation of the Croats to the situation in 1993 and in 1995, after the Washington Agreements and in fact, to this very day, because according to the indictment, Croatia had tried to partition Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout this period, and to annex parts of that country to Croatia, but at any rate, I will continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In light of your humanitarian work did you receive any commendations or any signs of gratitude from Bosniaks for your work?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If I knew that it would become such an important issue I would have kept more of them. I got some from Bosniaks, some from Croats and some that were given to me jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What were your relations with Alija Izetbegovic or official relations through you from -- between Zagreb and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Very good, and very fair. Just as they are supposed to be between statesmen and an ambassador accredited to that state. Unlike other ambassadors, I met with him quite often and with other members of the Presidency, either together or separately, because at that time it was a period of very lively activity because we signed a number of agreements, annexes to agreements that were signed pursuant to the Dayton peace accords because it was signed just after I came into office. That was the agreement on the special relations between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and on the basis of this agreement, which was in itself based on the Dayton peace accords, more than 30 annexes had to be drafted regulating some issues of mutual interest, from cross border cooperation, the issue of transport, traffic, trade, assistance in cases of natural disasters, and a number of other agreements. So I had to meet members of the Presidency quite often, and I cooperated with them very -- it was a very fair relation, and also with the members of the government of the federation, the majority of them were Bosniaks, but I was able to cooperate with them very well, and I had fond memories of these two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the then president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, awarded a decoration to Alija Izetbegovic and Haris Silajdzic, do you know when and how?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It was done before I came into office when the two states signed an agreement on friendship and cooperation, and Mr. Izetbegovic received the highest order. I think it is called the Order of King Dmitar Zvonimir with a sash. It is the highest decoration that is awarded only to statesmen. And this was covered by the media. It was on TV quite often. So myself, like all the other citizens, I was able to see that. I think it happened in Split, in the beginning of 1995. And I think that Mr. Haris Silajdzic was also awarded this decoration because he was the Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, any direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Mr. President. I think that some things perhaps need to be clarified. But my colleague mostly asked all the questions that I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Zoric, for all the international activities and the passing of the decisions and all the decisions relevant for international law, who is in charge -- who is entitled to pass such decisions in the Republic of Croatia? If this is not too difficult a question for you in legal terms, because I have to be quite general.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There was the constitutional and legal jurisdiction for the executive decision. It was the government. But all the agreements had to be ratified by the Croatian diet, the parliament, so all the international agreements had to be ratified by the Croatian diet, and a number of these agreements, that pertained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It seems to me that Mr. Krsnik's question is not relevant to the case at all. We are too far away from the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe this question is not relevant. Maybe he will follow up a question which is relevant to this case. Let us hear what is the follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So does the President of the state and the party that -- in the Republic of Croatia is able -- are they able to make a decision such as the decision to send the military forces to another state without the approval of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No. Before the.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I wonder if our witness has a legal background just to give evidence on purely legal issues. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this witness is a member of the parliament. He could testify in that capacity of the decisions adopted during that period. I think this is the qualification for this witness who testified on this question. Of course, this Tribunal will weigh the evidence given by this witness in the later stage. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, it is claimed here that the President Tudjman and the HDZ made the decision to send the Croatian Army to Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to annex the HZ HB to Croatia. Even if they had wanted to do that, could they have done that without the approval of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The statement of the high representative of the UN in Sarajevo, General Klein was disseminated quite recently. He reminded the public about various offers from the then Bosniak leadership to President Tudjman to take Herzegovina and to let the rest of BiH go its own way. As you know, this highly credible, and I think respectable, person does not talk out of turn, and he also stated, I think it was about a month ago, that the offer was rejected, that it was never accepted. And also, we have some recent statements by President Izetbegovic and his associates that this was just a tactical move to embroil Croatia in another type of game where, in my mind at least, it would never, ever be able to liberate its own occupied territories, Vukovar and Knin because some other principles would have applied in that case. Had Croatia done something like that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how then would it have been able to liberate its own territories that were held by Serbs at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did the Croatian parliament ever discuss or make any decisions authorising the Croatian Army to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No. Quite clearly no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Questions are asked here about ranks. Was the Croatian diet responsible for adopting a law on ranks in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when was this law passed?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a military man so I would not be able to give you an exact answer but I believe it was rather early, that is sometime in 1992 that this matter was regulated by law. Croatia once a republic in a different state, it did not have its own army. The army of the former country was predominantly Serb and when non-Serb members left it, it became completely Serb. It sided with Milosevic, so that in 1991, Croatia had to create its own army, and it was formed from some three elements. On one hand from those men who joined in and who in the early operations were volunteers, and who showed their value. And on the other hand, there were also people who came out from the former JNA, who were therefore designated to certain posts in that new army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I have to remind you to slow down because whatever you say will be translated in into the other two languages. The interpreters were far behind you. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I asked you this because it is suggested here that the ranks in the Croatian Army were given to people without any military education simply because they were close to the policies, be it of President Tudjman or the HDZ. Who is it that -- who were people who were conferred the ranks by the decision of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There were many, many people but President Tudjman was the commander of the army by definition and as any Supreme Commander he would select his command staff, but basically, people who in 1991 participated in the war and had success in that war first doing it without any ranks, later on there were also conferred upon certain ranks. A large number of people got those ranks some of them were reserve ranks but not all the ranks had to do with the military. They could belong to the military medical personnel. They could be administrative, personnel and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Perhaps we -- there is discerning with us, but was there a law, a decision taken by the diet conferring ranks upon people who were not members of the army, such as, for instance, the leader of your opposition party?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was a member of the government, and as a member of the cabinet, he was conferred a rank because it was a wartime government and it was somehow deemed that everybody who was at war and everybody who had to do something with the war should also have a military rank. And the same then held true of the -- of the President of my former party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And two more questions, --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: But excuse me, one cannot really say that the ranks were conferred upon people because of some closeness to. These were important matters, and these things were visible. They were visible to everybody. The whole public was aware of that. Nobody could be appointed high military officer without its meeting with its reflection in the public. So these things were not -- so these were serious matters and I suppose were treated as such. After all our former president of the republic was a military man himself. He had the highest military rank in the former army, so that he was a very strict person, and I really doubt that it might happen anything, that any slipshod decisions, any sloppy moves, could have been made in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you mean the former president, you mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I mean President Tudjman who was the youngest general at the time when Yugoslavia was liberated from fascism. He was the youngest Tito's general so he had military experience behind him. He was the head of the personnel department in Belgrade for a number of years, and he therefore knew very well, he had to know, he could not but know the procedure and I do not -- I'm not aware of any case that perhaps military rank was conferred upon somebody who did not deserve it. After all, all these matters were very serious and it was thank to his skills he won this war, which was not all that easy and there were many people who were saying that it would crumble away in two or three weeks time because he had to confront an army which was the fourth strongest army in Europe and in 1991 we didn't have all that many weapons, but I know this is an old story, I do not know whether we have to start this story all over again but Croatia was disarmed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the dual citizenship, since were you an ambassador, do you know how many Muslim Bosniaks obtained Croatian nationality and this especially applies to high SDA officials?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: A very large number of people were granted that nationality in Sarajevo. One might speak even of several thousand such individuals, and members of their families, after all, spent the war, the years, the war years, and that -- I mean members of families of high officials, be it state or military, lived in Zagreb, and the very fact that they spent five years in Croatia already entitled them to the Croatian nationality. Many of them applied for it and were given it, not only a large number of politicians but also public figures, sportsmen, media stars and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
