utterances.text: Well, much larger numbering of ordinary people. Much larger number. One could speak perhaps about 30 or so thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And at the time of elections in Croatia, and I mean Bosniak Muslims with Croatian nationality can they participate in the Croatian elections?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Every national may participate in the elections because that is one of the fundamental rights. When the elections are taking place abroad, then the poling stations are at places agreed with the relevant state. In Bosnia-Herzegovina we organised these elections at the time when I was the ambassador there by getting the consent, by getting the consent of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those elections were organised in various official places, that is in the embassy, in consular offices, so that we have a large number of our citizens, of our nationals, and for practical reasons we requested such a consent. We simply sought authorisation to be provided with additional polling stations in order to avoid crowding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right, right. The answer is important. They could vote. They could vote there in the elections held in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the other way around?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my final question. Perhaps I wasn't all that clear in the beginning. Namely -- of course it was not deliberate. When I said that you perhaps personally would have some knowledge of the presidential transcript, my question is whether you talked to people who were representatives of the diet boards or members of the government, why, and when was the decision taken to place all these documents, all these transcripts, under seal?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, I talked with, for instance, representative of the board for the home affairs and security in the diet. She is my personal friend and I know that everybody was upset about what was happening and that the coalition majority and the same holds true of the then opposition, that is representatives of the former power and amongst all of them, the opinion prevailed that law ought to be respected in the case of those papers, and that in some cases, when such papers appeared in public, that the judiciary in Croatia did not recognise their legal validity because their authenticity was not proven. I have no way of knowing that, but I know that people who were called upon to decide about that were very upset by it all and that is why it was decided that the law should be respected strictly and a procedure was prescribed concerning the storage of those documents in the Croatian state archives, and also, a special commission was appointed to then regulate the treatment of those documents and I believe this commission operates at the level of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the witness will clarify when it happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The question has been asked. When was this decision taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That decision was taken last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But the law on the archival -- on the archives acts, what was it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I think it has been in force since 1993 and if not since 1993, then there is another law regulating, stipulating that all the legal matters with the Croatia has failed to resolve by itself in its parliament as an independent state that in all such cases it would adopt the former legislation that is the legislation of the former state so that one can take it that from the very beginning, Croatia, as this matter has been regulated legally, even in the new state because Croatia took over and adopted all the legislation of the former state which was not contrary to its own legislation. So that there were no problems. There was an archives law which existed throughout the existence of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last and final question. If I told you -- if I told you that these transcripts turned up before this Court, could they turn up against the will and wishes of the diet or the government in conformity with the law?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: They could not turn up here if it was not done in a manner prescribed by law, and I do not know if that is the case. There is a procedure and you should know it, I do not know it, perhaps you do I do not know that but they could turn up here only if they were provided in the legally prescribed manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions. No, no, I'm sorry. I've also forgotten, I will now show you Exhibit D1/326 and D1/327. Could they please be given to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we can do it with both immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first exhibit, D1/326, this is the colour one, can you tell the Court what is that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: This is the publication which I mentioned, and where school children in Croatia are offered the summer school of foreign languages and that summer school is organised on the village of Obonjan in the facility where we used to accommodate refugees. These facilities were built for the accommodation of refugees there. And as it looks and what these buildings look like now, did they look like that when the refugees were there? Well more or less, except of course they were painted because when different people are there, I mean such buildings are pretty much ruined but there were no architectural changes. This refugee centre was refurbished, was furnished and organised, thanks to a special organisation which is called Gemeinschaft Fuer Technische Zusammenarbeit from Germany. It is a special office of the German government, and they helped us to do that. And now it is very suited for children. And this is this prospectus from the school. My son brought it to me because he wanted to go there and I guess he will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the other document, D1/327 it is in B/C/S as we call it here. Can you tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of gratitude and is signed 9th of January, 1993, and it has its official number. It was from the staff of the armed forces in Maglaj of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I had supplied them with some food and other items for the defence. Maglaj is a place south of Derventa or north of Zenica in the heart of Bosnia. And it was signed by Brigadier Sulejman Herceg therefore one can assume that he was a Bosniak. And Anto Marinac, commander of the HVO staff in Maglaj so judging by the name he's a Croat from Bosnia. I have several of such letters of gratitude but I have kept this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as for those photos, I see little probative values in this case. As for this letter, we need the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, of course, we shall translate it, in problem. It's not a big problem. It is not a big document. And as for Obonjan, I'm confused because a number of witnesses spoke about Obonjan and called it a camp, and I will write a motion and quote witnesses for the Prosecution who said that. And that is why I brought these photographs, to show you what kind of camp is it, and I wanted to tender it through this witness. That was the reason why I did it. And there were several witnesses who spoke about that. And the Prosecution is well aware of that. Thank you very much for coming here and helping the Chamber to come as close to the truth as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we have a couple of minutes just to distribute our exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a housekeeping matter I believe the witness just spoke about D1/327 as being a letter of gratitude. And in fact, that is in fact D1/326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the pictures are 1/327 so I just wanted to clear the record up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11090 to 11102.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, good afternoon, I'm trial attorney representing the Prosecution and I've got some questions to you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just to complete the story with these pictures, my question is: When did the last refugee leave the Obonjan island?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: As soon as the peek of the crisis was over. I'd say that in 1995, they were all gone by that time. That particular accommodation facility was used for a very short time, at least much less than a number of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And when this famous camp was opened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean the language camp, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It is written here international, some language camp. That's why I called it camp.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: That was a refugee centre open at the time when the refugee crisis in Croatia escalated. I already said that between March and April, we received more than 200.000 people, and that the figure doubled over the next two months, and then we had to open a number of such facilities because that is where we could accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, the question is a very simple one. That is when this camp was opened -- I mean the language institute opened. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry. I think it's been in operation for several years. I'm not really sure. But that place, that centre, existed throughout as a separate company. I mean it's an institution. And then for a while, we used this institution to accommodate people there, contrary to its original purpose, because we had no where else to put them, but aware of the predicament of those people, as soon as some other possibility presented itself, we took those people to some better places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions relevant to this picture. Mr. Zoric, just one question so far in respect of presidential transcripts. As far as I understood from your testimony, you were never present when the transcript, presidential transcripts, were being drafted, am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean, where they were drafted, when they were made. I suppose I was not in such an office to be there, and I simply do not know who made them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't have access to presidential transcripts, am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I think that nobody had access to presidential transcripts apart from persons authorised by statute, and also there was never a need to gain access to them, nor was there any knowledge about their existence. These transcripts have become the subject of the day over the past two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now let us put aside this issue. We will return to it if we have time in the beginning -- at the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to focus myself on Herzegovina issues, which are directly relevant to our case, because the rest of the issues are very well covered by the witness in his direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If it is correct what my learned friend is saying, then I do not know how -- what do -- does his cross-examination have to do with my direct examination? In my direct examination, there was not a single question that concerned the activities of Herceg-Bosna or humanitarian issues in Herceg-Bosna. This man was not responsible for work with refugees and expelled persons in Herceg-Bosna, but in Republic of Croatia, and my direct examination had to do with that and only with that. So what is the foundation for the cross-examination and when I go through this documents that were supplied by the Prosecution, we see that all these documents have to do with the work and operation of similar offices to the one in which Mr. Zoric worked in Herceg-Bosna, and I do not know what could be the foundation for such cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, during the testimony, the witness said that he was in charge of the overall humanitarian aid issues throughout that period and throughout that territory, which might include the branch office in Herzegovina. Let us see what kind of question the Prosecution will concentrate on, and at the same time, I have to remind the Prosecutor that your cross-examination should somehow relate to subject matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do my best, and of course I'm authorised to make questions according to rules of cross-examination relevant to the credibility of a witness, and of course, Herceg-Bosna is a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some of the refugees were from Herceg-Bosna, including refugees who were placed in Obonjan and other refugee centres. That's why -- that's the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, what exactly was your position called in the office of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The office was called the office of the government of the Republic of Croatia for displaced persons and refugees, and I was secretary-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was the head of the office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The head of the office was Dr. Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's agree on the following. In my questions, I will not give the full name of your office because it will take a while. Let's limit ourselves to the term "office" all right? Your office.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior as the general-secretary?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Adalbert Rebic. And above him in the government, men who coordinated these activities, and it was deputy Prime Minister, Dr. Mate Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who exactly were your functions as the general-secretary?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Organisation mostly, but that was the time when we couldn't really make strict assignments and be responsible for only one or another thing. In the early days we often worked during the state of alert, when lights went out, sometimes we wouldn't be able to go home because of the situation. We had to spend the night in our office so it is very difficult to say what were strictly the terms of reference. But generally speaking my task was to look after the organisation or rather to see how much flour we have, how do we get it, how we shall distribute that flour, how to get trucks to take it away, where to find money, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In one of the documents I came across person whose name is Josip Esterajher, correct? Excuse my pronunciation, "riner" or "rajher"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know who you mean. He is Josip Esterajher. He arrived from Vukovar. He managed to break through following the occupation of Vukovar and he worked there as a journalist, as a radio journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what was his position in your office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: His position was that I had him as my assistant because I simply needed a capable man to work with me, and he was my assistant. What he became later, when I left, I believe he headed some departments, but I was the one who hired him as my assistant. And he was -- he organised the media promotion of the office in his early days working with numerous journalists who arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, who else, apart from Mr. Rebic, was authorised to sign official documents coming out of your office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: For a while, Rebic had a deputy but it was already at the time when I was leaving the office, so that another person was brought in, and he helped him as his deputy. Since the volume of work has grown significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you authorised to sign documents for Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, if he -- yes, if I had his authorisation to do that, but I mostly signed some administrative papers, such as bills, or relations with people who worked in that office, and so on and so forth. That is, I was to organise the secretary's office there, organise work in that office and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the usher just to show to the witness two exhibits, that is 566.3, and 286.1. You should put both documents in front of the witness so that he could compare those two documents because original?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: This is not Dr. Rebic's signature. I saw his signature so many times. This is not his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you a question yet?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you have two documents in front of you. Both documents are drafted, made, just in the name of Mr. Rebic, but as far as I see, they are signed by different people, am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I didn't get the chance to see the second document, but this signature is not the signature by Mr. Rebic and I also have to warn you of the fact that we had a large number of forgeries at that time and that we handed these forgeries to the police, quite often we did issue such papers but whether these papers are credible or not, it is really hard to say on the basis of a photocopy. We had so many cases of documents being forged and we always asked the police to investigate these matters. These talk -- such documents were issued when the family of people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you're not answering my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it really would be fair for the witness to be allowed to complete his explanation, because I think that the issue of the forgeries of document is quite important. I think it would be fair to let him finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness should answer the question first. Then, if he need to explain to the Prosecutor, he may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not ask a question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question you asked is that they are signed by the different people, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My next question is what document are you talking about? What document do you have in front of you now? Just tell me the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: My answer pertains to both documents, both documents that I have in my hand. I tried to tell you how such documents were issued, and I also wanted to warn you that people forged such documents quite often. The document bearing number 101547467 indicates quite clearly that this is a document sent to somebody living in Zagreb. The address is had much street number 2. I assume that this is a person who sought permission to house some refugees in his own home. We issued such approvals as the office in charge of such matters, and that also meant that we would take upon ourselves to fulfil some needs of these people, because then such people would arrive to Croatia and seek other status, not refugee status. That meant that we would have to assume other obligations. And as the office in charge of these matters, we had to issue our approval. And we had to suggest to other authorities, relevant authorities, such as the border police, to let a person into Croatia or not. If somebody stated that they wanted to come to Croatia as the -- as a refugee, coming from a village or a town called Siroki Brijeg, I wouldn't sign such an approval because that town remained free throughout the war, and there was no reason for a person to flee such a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much but let's agree on the following. It's a cross-examination. Normally the questions are very brief and the responses should be brief. If I need your explanations, I will ask you, by all means, or if the judges need explanations, they will ask you. But no need to make explanations to each question, unless you're asked to do that. I'm sorry. Otherwise, we'll never complete our cross-examination. I'm sorry. But is that signature familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I have already said what my view of the signature is. I am quite suspicious of it. I do know the person to whom this -- whose signature this purports to be. He is a priest. And he really have my doubts. I have already said that there have been numerous cases of abuse that have all been referred to the police for their investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already said what I wanted to say. In his first answer, when he was asked to express his view of the signature, he said that he might be able to give a better answer if he were shown the original of the signature. And then he would be better able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in doubt now if we should go for a break or not, because my learned colleagues are making some signs to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we might have a break for 20 minutes. So we will resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, let's pass on to the second document. Do you have it in front of you? That's Exhibit 566.3. Witness, is it correct that this document is signed by someone else for Mr. Rebic? Do you know the person to whom this signature belongs?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was authorised to sign documents for Mr. Rebic in August, 1993? Did he have a deputy at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the fact that 80 per cent of the documents in this binder are new documents, documents that have not been admitted by this Trial Chamber, we see that the first document has the stamp of the Zagreb archive, yet the second one does not have any stamp indicating its origin so could we please establish the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it is on the list provided by the Prosecution, could you see that this document was provided by that person himself, which is on the second page of the whole binder. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know who signed it, and -- but I can see from this document that a person seeking the issuing of this document indicating that he was travelling from Bosnia to Slovakia, through Slovenia. At that time the persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina were unable to enter Slovenia without a visa. They needed a visa. And the same went for many other European countries, they were unable to get into these countries without a visa. And since we were unable to find accommodation for such refugees, they sought approval to go to third countries or perhaps they went to such countries on a business trip. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let's put aside these exhibits and go on with our cross-examination. So, Witness, you just told me that you were in charge of, let's say, general questions, organisations of functioning of your office, right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the communication of your office with corresponding offices in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Herceg-Bosna and third countries?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the corresponding offices would be, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean the same offices, offices for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, our contacts with them were quite scarce because it was difficult to establish such contacts, because despite the fact that the distance was not great, there would be a number of battle fields separating us, so communications were very difficult at that time, particularly in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And were you in charge of -- sorry, refugee centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In a way, yes, I was in charge. I had to make sure that the costs were met and to pay for the salaries of the people working in those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But was there anyone else in your office who was, let's say -- whose functions were, let's say, limited to controlling of functioning of centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There were about 30 of us working in the office. There was a section that was in charge of it. There were five or six people there. They took care of the logistics in such centres. I think that those people still continue to perform this job. Unfortunately. Because I think that there are still some 30.000 people who have been unable to go back and they are still housed in one or another of those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why I ask this question because I'm -- I've got a summary in front of me, and the summaries just -- issued on the 15th of April, and according to the summaries, you were also head of the refugee camps in the Republic of Croatia. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, I could not have been the head of the refugee camps because I was already a member of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, maybe it was a slip of my tongue. I'm talking about the summaries of your potential testimony in court. Summary of 15th of April, 2002, sorry if I have misled someone here. So I would like to clarify this situation. Were you the head of the camps or not, in 1993 -- the head of the camps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, until spring, but every centre had its own manager. We had 596 facilities where we housed people. So it was impossible for a single person to run almost 600 of such centres. Some were in the process of being closed down. Some were opened up recently. But the -- there were always quite a few people housed there, and there was a person who was managing such centres always. And we always tried to ensure the participation of the people who were housed there. So they had their own tasks and roles. People who wanted to work in the kitchen or if some of them were experts, I don't know, teachers, then they would be given this job. So in effect they managed the centres themselves, and we from Zagreb merely made sure that they had enough food, to provide dermatological care, in other words to protect the outbreak of any diseases, to meet their costs and the electricity bills and food bills and so on, to pay for the funerals and organise funerals and things like that, as I have already said, but I would really be hard put to manage almost 600 such places. Every place had its own manager or if there were some smaller locations, then one person would be in charge of several. But we were the office at the level of the government that took care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mean the spring of 1993? I'm looking just in the transcript, "Yes, until spring." Do you mean spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I believe that it was sometime in April that I left the office because I was elected to the diet. So I had to become -- take my post in the parliament because I became the -- one of the deputy speakers of the -- of the parliament. And it was also impossible for somebody to be in the executive and in the legislature at the same time so I had to leave my previous office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So when did you exactly did you leave your office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well it's really difficult for me to say because it's been eight years. I think it was April 1993. I think that's specific enough because I didn't know this date would become so important. But at any rate it was in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You were talking about legislation that was adopted in Croatia in respect of refugees and displaced persons. Could you just clear up when exactly that legislation was adopted?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At first we had just a decree that was issued by the government. That was in 1991. And also for a part of 1992. But decrees had a limited period of validity so that the government had to extend its period of validity in accordance with its competence, and since the decrees also had to be amended and improved, they were amended accordingly and I think that in 1992 or 1993, they were adopted as a law, in accordance with the international standards governing this area. I'm referring to the treatment of the refugees, asylum seekers and displaced persons. Also another law was passed later regulating the issue of humanitarian aid, who is entitled to deliver such aid, which items are -- can be delivered, duty-free or free of customs, to prevent any possible abuses in this respect, but at any rate, these two laws governed this area. And all the other regulations and laws valid in the Republic of Croatia were also enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that somewhere in February, 1993, your office announced that all refugees in Croatia would be registered or were registered in February from the 10th of February to the 28th of February?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It's quite likely that the dates are correct, because we conducted the census and the registration of refugees on several occasions, to be able to determine precisely who they are, where they come from, and where they are housed. They came in a rather chaotic manner, overnight, several tens of thousands would arrive. Some of them went on their own initiative and -- to the third countries, abroad. They left one facility to go to another. They failed to deregister. So we simply had to know what we had on our hands. The records sometimes did not reflect the actual situation. I mean the population. And I think at that time 12 per cent of the overall population in Croatia consisted of refugees or displaced persons. It would be equal to 35 million people with the refugee status in the United States of America. That would be the same ratio. Croatia was a small country and we had to carry out this census. We got really quite correct data from the census and it helped us to organise ourselves and to organise the return, to prepare for the return of the refugees when -- once it became possible. And other censuses were carried out later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: According to the legislation, I mean the laws that were valid at that time, for what period of time the status of refugee was granted?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The refugee status, according to our law and according to the laws of other countries is a temporary form of protection so that it was granted for a period of six months, and if after the expiry of the six-month period, if the conditions that have led the person to become a refugee still existed, in other words if the area from which he or she came was still occupied, if he still had reasons to fear, in other words if all these reasons which led him to become a refugee still existed, his refugee status was extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But is it correct that the announcement that was made by your office limited the status of refugees to three months?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't think I could confirm that. I do not think that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. Why I'm claiming that, if a few minutes I will show you a document which -- from where I took this information. But was it also announced by your office that all refugees or displaced -- and displaced persons were supposed to go through a new registration?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. We took that decision because it was absolutely necessary, whenever I travelled it a foreign country requiring a visa, then they authorised me to go there for seven days. I recently went to the United States and it said -- and my visa said exactly how many days I could spend there. I had to show it to immigration authorities. To Croatia, people came for different reasons. Some were refugees, some came on business and some people were just crossing and going to third countries. For instance, nobody could go to Austria through Bosnia-Herzegovina without passing through Croatia. In order to make sure that everybody really enjoyed the status he was to have, we needed to register those people and issue them with relevant documents. All people that were registered were also issued with identity documents, with a photographs among other things in order to avoid any misuse, because there were such cases. I have to repeat that. The refugees staying in this country are also issued about identity documents and are registered upon their arrival. Moreover, the files of third countries, that is countries which came to Croatia and took over certain quotas of refugees, which matched their registration procedures, were much stricter, when representatives of the Red Cross from some western countries came to Croatia to register refugees, then they would provide with asylum, with temporary shelter in their country, they took down many more particulars than we did, and that included medical examinations. I can tell you that they never took over sick persons. They left them to us to care for them. So that we had to -- some 30 odd facilities where we look after persons who had been abandoned by everybody, and that includes Croats, Muslims and some Serbs from BH, and from Croatia. And who could not get temporary protection in third countries. I suppose that is what their laws were like, much stricter than ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, please concentrate on the questions asked by the Prosecution. If he needs more information, he will ask you the following questions. Just give a very concise answer to the questions. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it true that there were some unlicensed refugee centres which were supposed to be closed after that statement made by your office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were, and we managed to close down most of such facilities because these facilities did not provide even the minimal conditions, either sanitary or any other, to accommodate people. They did not have any electricity supply or the voltage was too low. They would have no bathrooms or something. And we then closed them down and moved them to other temporary facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 243, just page 6. I must warn my learned colleagues that we have a B/C/S translation of the relevant part of this document. You will find it just in the end of this exhibit. So Mr. Usher, I would like you also to check the translation just after the last page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see that the English document has 15 pages, and I still cannot find -- I cannot find the translation of the document. I'm really trying very hard but I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It's at the end of this document, just check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if Mr. Prosecutor can help us, does he wants to say that only these five sentences were translated out of these 15 pages of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, because the rest of the pages, the rest of the information is not relevant to Croatia at all. That's why no need to overstrain our resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I know enough English to see in English say, "Prisoners and detainees, refugees, health matters, local Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the Prosecutor is directing our attention to the specific paragraph that is paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then you could have produced it also in English, only that particular passage, to produce it in English and then just say which document it came from. Here we have a whole document, so it would have been fair to have the whole document translated so that we can see that nothing has been taken out of the context, and it would be fair to show the whole document to the witness, because it is an integral part of a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed on the basis of the document provided for us by the Prosecution, and later on, this Trial Chamber will judge whether there is a need to translate the whole document into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the translation of the document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what complete document you are talking about but I do have some piece of translation, some information, some text, about refugees in Croatia, which says that the refugees will be registered between the 10th and 28th of February, after which they will have refugee status for three months. And that anyone not registered will be treated as a foreigner. This means that the law on the movement and residence of foreigners will apply to them. There is such a law in Croatia. And according to it -- and it stipulates the conditions under which people can stay in Croatia. I do not know what is the Bosnian government in Croatia. We also referred it to the government of BH. So this is not -- this is atypical terminology, and, yes, we did seek the channel from which we could use to get the official authorities in Sarajevo tell us which were -- which areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina were safe so that we wouldn't have to admit people from those areas, also if it is some municipality which was free and safe, and we didn't know about it in Zagreb, then why would people from there come to Croatia and say, "We are refugees"? It would lack sense. That is why we wanted them to tell us these areas are vulnerable. We wanted the official authorities in Sarajevo to tell us which areas in that country are affected by war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the question is concentrated on the time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And witness, I must explain to you this is an ECMM report dated the 7th of February, 1993, on humanitarian activity. And this passage is taken from this report. And let's return to the problem of these maybe misinterpretation of three months or six months. So did you give them -- I mean to the refugees and displaced persons, three or six months to solve all their problems?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: They had to report every month to have their status extended, and it was extended invariably. It is completely irrelevant whether they were granted a status for three months or six months because this is a technical issue, and if that period of time, three months or six months, expired, and somebody would still have to be treated as a refugee, then the status would be extended. We have refugees in Croatia to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And anyone not registered shall be treated as a foreigner. Maybe you will brief a little bit the Trial Chamber what is the difference between the status of refugee and foreigner, according to your legislation that was valid at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There is a big difference. If you recognise the status of refugee to someone in your country then you are bound to provide him with accommodations, schooling for the children, medical treatment, and all the rest that is necessary so that such a person is taken care of for life. If somebody is only a foreigner in this country, then he must bear the costs if he falls ill, then he must pay the costs of his treatment. If he doesn't have accommodation, then he has to go to a hotel. Then he's a foreigner. If he's come there to study, to -- then there are again regulations which say under which conditions they may be allowed to do that. And the law on aliens in the Republic of Croatia, all these conditions are strictly specified from studies to treatment to specialization to so and so forth. At that time in Croatia, if I'm interpreting it correctly, without any visa, without any authorisation, one could live for three months in Croatia. After that, one needed a visa. In many countries, that was much more strict and -- but I repeat, Croatia was a country at war at the time and 12 per cent of its population had the refugee status. For a country much 4 million, I repeat, it is equal as 35 million would be in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. But do citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina need a visa to cross the Croatian border? Let's say in 1993, from the beginning, until the period of time when you were still in office.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Not only then. Croatia is the only country, the only European country, in which the nationals of -- into which the nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina can enter without a visa. To this day, they cannot go anywhere with a BH passport without a visa. Not even to Slovenia. Only they can come and they could come to Croatia without a visa throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But do soldiers of, let's say, ABiH and HVO need some sort of safe conduct to cross the border of your state at this same period of time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: As soldiers, they could not come to Croatia. As private persons, yes. I have already said that the Sarajevo authorities asked us not to grant the status of refugees to able-bodied persons, and it often placed us before a two-edged sword because if we recognised refugee status to somebody then that person would enjoy the international protection and the UNHCR protection. It was not up to us to judge who is able-bodied in Bosnia and who isn't. That was that country's business but at meetings in Zagreb, President Izetbegovic very often requested that an end be put to the reception of refugees who are capable of defending their country, and all we could do was convert it into a moral appeal to people to go back to their country. But if members of an able-bodied BH national had been granted the refugee status in Croatia, his wife and children, then we had absolutely no possibility whatsoever to refuse such a person, the father of the family, because under the international humanitarian law we also had to respect the request for joining families. So many people who didn't feel like fighting in BH used that, and we had no way of preventing it, nor did we prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My next question is, according to this document, just your office promised that more suitable accommodation will be found for the refugees. What did you mean by "more suitable accommodation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let the Prosecutor ask a more correct question. It says very clearly here, "And all unlicensed refugee centres", "unlicensed centres, will be closed." Refugee centres which are unlicensed. And all you said were refugee centres which are not suitable enough. And it is suggested that these were centres without proper conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must respond to this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, read that sentence from, "In addition" to the end and put your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We already talked about unlicensed refugee centres. And now my question is the second part of this sentence. What did they mean by "more suitable accommodations" in comparison with those unlicensed and closed centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I shall be very happy to answer that, sir. In the summer of 1992, on the main railway station -- at the main railway station in Zagreb, for a month, there were two trains with several thousand women and children. Those were trains in which people had arrived from Bosnia before the bridge across the Sava was demolished in Samac or Brod. No other neighbouring state allowed those trains to go there. And people who were in them wanted to draw attention to themselves, and refused to be moved from those trains. So you can well imagine the sanitary conditions in a train at the main railway station, in a train which is stationary for a month, and all the dangers it carries. And they were such about 30 such facilities. They would spring up overnight. People perhaps were not responsible for that because they did not know who to turn to. And perhaps of their own, they organised their accommodation perhaps in some sheds, some shacks, in some abandoned areas, but in a facility which houses 50 and when you have electrical installations for 50 people, you can't simply have 1.000 people. So there was constantly a danger of fire in some of these facilities. And it was primarily for reasons of hygiene that these people needed to be transferred to some organised facilities, to some other facilities, which we provided together with the international organisations. A number of such locations for refugee accommodation from 1991 onward were furnished by international humanitarian organisations in order to accommodate the refugees. That means suitable, adequate, proper accommodation. All those words can be used for the Croatian word which says Priclandon [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, thank very much but I would like to limit my question to 1993, after this decision was announced. I mean in March, April, 1993, what kind of new, more suitable accommodations were created?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, facilities in Varazdin. It is a town 60 kilometres from Zagreb. There in the centre of town were two large barracks used by the former army. They were left empty and we refurbished it them and thus had adequate accommodations there, and the logistics possibilities in that centre. And there we moved people who, until then, had lived under inhumane conditions, in some make shift areas. And the same happened in Pula or for instance in Karlovac. It was something that was absolutely necessary. And whoever saw that accommodation could only be astounded by some of the things. In some holiday homes, for instance, some holiday centres, workers holiday centres, there was no sewage, for instance, in some of that. And three years later, after three years of the refugees' life in them, the conditions simply became unbearable, and then they had to be moved. Some resisted those moves. That is true. Perhaps because they engaged in prostitution and had some additional sources of income because we had such cases too. Prostitution not only in the centre itself but also in the -- in the town, in the place where the centre was. And that is an illicit activity and a very dangerous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's abstain from the problem of prostitution now and go on to the centres still. What about the refugee centre in Gasinci and Korcula? Were they new refugee centres? And when were they set up?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The refugee centre at Gasinci had much was set up after the fall of Vukovar. They were people who came from east Slavonia. And since it was a very spacious area, we could accommodate there several thousand people so that to all intensive purposes it was a large Bosnian town. Before that, Gasinci was a military training area, where one took general -- when one took tests to become a general in the Yugoslav People's Army. The Yugoslav People's Army used to be there and it had all the conditions for the accommodation of a large number of people, a large kitchen, a large canteen, a school, infirmary, play grounds, and there were fishing ponds. They are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: And as for Korcula, I really cannot say when that started, because the facilities in Dalmatia were former tourist resorts, tourist facilities so I presume that was the case of Korcula. But I repeat we had about 600 different facilities. I cannot be quite sure. Gasinci, I know it because it was the first large centre we started, and we spent quite a lot of money to reconvert it and adapt it for the new purposes for refugees, and there were several international organisations active there throughout and that includes the UNHCR, the International red cross and so on and so forth. Almost 30.000 people passed through that centre during its operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And in what cases, the people who were living on the territory of the Republic of Croatia -- I mean displaced persons, refugees -- were subject to repatriation, according to this announcement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Displaced persons who were not subject to repatriation, they were subject to return home. And they could go home when their areas became free, but until 1995, when the largest part of Croatia, hitherto occupied, were liberated, we did not register a single return. We only began to see more and more expulsions. And it was only 2001 that they could return. Where could they it go in? To devastated areas, to mined areas, that is without reconstruction, so it took another two or three years during which it was impossible to return. And besides, during -- if you live as a refugee for six or seven years, so many things change in your life, children grow up, got used to living in one place, they already left, it's very difficult for them to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My next question will be, you just stated today that at some point, you were engaged in the problems of granting citizenship.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No, no. I had nothing to do with that, except that like everybody else I had to go through a procedure before the authorities issuing passports. No, I didn't play any role there. Perhaps it was a misunderstanding. I apologise if there was one, but no, all the matters relative to nationality to citizenship are within the mandate of the Ministry of the Interior, and as an ambassador, if that is what you mean, I could perhaps recommend some persons from the countries to which I had been accredited, I could recommend certain persons be admitted into Croatian nationality. They came to us and we would then forward their applications to Zagreb, with or without our recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But were you aware of the problems of granting citizenship in the period of time when you were holding your office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what problems you mean and who would have these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will clarify. How long did the procedure of getting citizenship of the Republic of Croatia normally take, let's say, in 1993, when you were in office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I did not seek -- I did not apply for citizenship at that time. I already had the citizenship. I guess it's very simple thing. Those who had the citizenship of the -- one of the republics, as that existed in the former state, if they had permanent residence or if they were born in the Republic of Croatia, they were granted Croatian citizenship. Those who had come from other republics, who had temporary residence in the Republic of Croatia, to them the appropriate, relevant provisions of the law on citizenship in the Republic of Croatia applied. And I'm really not competent to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, if you can't, you can't. Now, let's pass on to another subject. That's the problem of just moving of people to the third countries. Did it take place in the time when you were in the office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, while I was in the office, people went to third countries. Some went on their own initiative, they organised it, their family members who were already in those countries sent letters of guarantee to them. One couldn't get into some of the countries, for instance, Germany, without a letter of guarantee issued by somebody who would be able to take care of you. But in some cases, it happened that, for instance, the Netherlands or Denmark would send special trains where several thousands of people would be selected and then taken to those countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you told today that in any case, most of the people who were leaving for third countries were crossing the territory of the Republic of Croatia, right? What kind of documents did they need at that time just to have this right to cross the territory -- the border in and cross it out?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: They needed some kind of a letter of guarantee, if they wanted to be taken care of in Croatia. We approved what they said they would do. If somebody said, "I travel from place X to Budapest," then we would confirm that this person was indeed travelling to Budapest. For us that meant that that person would not cheat us, that he would not stay in Split saying, "I have a chronic illness and now you have a duty to accept me as a refugee and put me in one of your hospitals." We couldn't do that because we already had a large number of people who had that status. And in mid-1992, Croatian government urged the western countries to accept more refugees. I'm not a military strategist but my feeling was that the aggressor wanted to smother those areas that he could not reach with his artillery, with refugees, to send as many refugees to these areas, paralysing the rear so to speak, so that for instance in the town of Makarska which is on the Croatian coast quite close to the border, we would have twice as many refugees than the original inhabitants, in some periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of refugees didn't get into the transcript. The number is 700.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see any number on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask about the so-called transit visa. Did you have transit visa at that period of time? And for how long, if they existed, they were valid?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No. There were no transit visas, and there is no piece of paper indicating that it is the transit visa. I know from my experience in consular affairs what a transit visa is. There were letters of recommendation or something like that. That was always sought by the family members or somebody -- some other interested party. And then the -- that person would be able to identify himself. That was a way to specify who that person was and where that person was going. It was a weird situation. You would receive 10.000 refugees one day, and then the next day, you would receive a delegation of businessmen and you would try to cut a deal with them of some kind. So there has to be a difference between the two. But, sir, we were very much aware of the fact that we were the first country of call, the first asylum country. I got an explanation about that from the UNHCR. And the first asylum countries have certain obligations that other countries do not have. Other countries were very much afraid of the great influx of refugees. France, for instance, did not want to accept any refugees in an organised way. They accepted only those who went there on their own initiative. That was a big problem during the conferences, international conference in Geneva. I know what the problem was. Germany had accepted the largest number of refugees and they wanted other European countries to share the burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I wonder all those questions is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I think that all these questions are relevant to the case because it's just the period of time, 1993, when the war started, and just in the end of the stay of our witness in his office, the situation was, as he explained to us, and it's quite possible that after that, the situation changed, with the beginning of this armed conflict between the HVO and the BiH. That's why I asked so, let's say, closely him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we know that there are a lot of refugees during the period of war at that time coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia. We know that. There is no dispute about that. So what's the point for your cross-examination on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, just taking into consideration the period of time when the witness was in the office of displaced persons and refugees, I must say that I'm about to complete my cross-examination now, and all the questions which will be relevant to some other periods of time may be asked, if other witnesses appear here before the Court room and maybe then I will try to compare the situation. That's what the idea of my cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief. You have in fact anticipated my objection. Rule 90(h) (ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence states that in the cross-examination of a witness, counsel should put to the witness the nature of the case of the party so if the Prosecutor is attacking this witness regardless of whether he is trying to impeach him or contradict the contents of his testimony, then let him say that he does not agree with his statement that Croatia accepted refugees, but after all, you, Your Honours, have just said that the Trial Chamber is very much aware of that, and that you do not see the point of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. You may continue your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Should I answer the objection, first of all, I think? Should I give my response to the objection by the defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may do that but we are not debating on the legal issues at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: That's if this was an objection, what was the point of the examination-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the Defence counsel raised an objection concerning your cross-examination on that point, and you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour. I will conclude my cross-examination with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the judges? Yes, Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. During your testimony, Witness, you spoke about what the refugees could exchange -- and I'd like -- you said that you are a cultural anthropologist and I'd like to draw on that knowledge. I heard one word very often here which you did not use today but I'm quite sure you know what it means and perhaps you can tell me and you can tell me if that word was used in those exchanges that you told us between the refugees that you saw them and whether you saw any -- whether they reflected some animosity between Muslims and Croats who lived together in those camps. Did you hear any such word, any such exchange?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the word, and I believe I know what its origin is. It is -- which is the word balija, and it had historically different meaning from the one that it has today. Once upon a time, perhaps centuries ago, it meant a group within several Muslim communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it meant a kind of the lowest stratum of that society, mostly those who raised sheep somewhere in the mountains so that the Muslims in towns called them balijas. It was pejorative word but it mostly was an indication of their social status. Later on, the pejorative meaning of that word was taken over by the population of the other two peoples, and that was a kind of a deprecating word they used when referring to Muslims. Generally speaking, in those different areas, there is no ethnic community or -- I mean you do not find a single ethnic which doesn't have some bad, some derogatory term for the other two people. So that some of the more primitive members of those communities would use the term balijas for Muslims, but that term originated within their own ranks to refer to the lowest stratum of their own society and I believe it is of Persian origin it was used during conflicts, yes, it was but there were surprisingly few of them. In view of the situation that prevailed in their own countries. I mean, these people were never so isolated that they could not watch the news from the areas they had come from. Very often they were accommodated together or very near. I explained why they had to be separated at times. So that at times, there were certain tensions which I tried to calm down and also, if I made add, with regard to what the Prosecutor asked, whether after the conflict in BH between the Muslims and Croats there were some changes in our attitude to refugees, I must most emphatically say that no, that our attitude to them did not change and in all the logistics were still supplied from Croatia for them, all the time, until the end of the war, and personally, later on, as a MP, I was the one who led several convoys to Tuzla. Tuzla was never a town with a Bosnian Croat majority or the controlled by the HVO because it was the army of BH which controlled it. And yet I took them all the way from the Adriatic coast there, and those were very dangerous trips. Had my attitude or anyone's attitude to those refugees changed, somebody in Sarajevo would have begrudged me that and very seriously. And as you know, there were three sides. And if you side with any of the sides more than is normal, then that is -- then it is viewed wrongly by others. So that despite all the psychological burden, and I repeat psychological, mental burden, because it wasn't easy to watch reports about massacres of Croats, and there were an a number of them too, we nevertheless in spite of all that, we tried to calm, to placate people and to calm the situation. So on a number of occasions, I led delegations to Bosnia and I was the first deputy of the Croatian diet who attended Bugojno in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I think you answered the question which bothered me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of judge's question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give evidence. We all wish you good luck in your future. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to ask, through you, the Prosecutor, as regards -- as regards document P566.3, I would like you to instruct the Prosecutor to tell me how he came to -- into possession of this document from Mr. Rizvanbegovic, and if there is a statement from Mr. Rizvanbegovic as to the way in which he came into contact with the Prosecutor and how he gave the document to the Prosecutor, all the more so because the witness stated that this document might be a forgery, or indeed he stated that it was a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you know, we -- well, I think the Prosecution will tell you more information about the source of this document, but for a document to be used in this courtroom, we only want the establishment of the minimum foundations of that document, because that is the cross-examination. Let us hear whether there is anything more the Prosecution would like to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: The only thing that I can tell the Trial Chamber that we received this document from the person who indicated in the document. Whether we took witness statements from him or not, I think I'm not obliged to answer to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this name has been mentioned and used in this courtroom, I think that they are obliged, because, as the Defence has been claiming for a very long time, it would be very important to find out why this person gave this certificate and what he testified about, because I keep saying here that this trial is full of -- that many of the documents proffered are forgeries and that many of the testimonies are influenced by the AID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a very serious allegation, Mr. Krsnik. If you have some objections to the admission of certain documents, you are entitled to make those objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will make. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this moment, I would like to ask you whether you have any documents to tender through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the two documents that were tendered, D1/326 and D1/327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I think that this picture is not relevant at all. As for the second document, it was not translated. I was unable to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think I have expressed my view on those two documents. One is not translated. We are waiting for the translation. The other one, I believe the pictures add very little probative value to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, fortunately I have a very good memory and I do know what the Prosecution witnesses have been saying. For the Defence, this is of great probative value, except if the Trial Chamber has already formed its view on the witnesses testifying about the conditions of the -- at the Obonjan facility. If some of the witnesses - now I can't recall their pseudonyms - if they were saying that this area was like a concentration camp, I will use up this evening to look up these witnesses. So I just wanted you to see -- for the head of that office to confirm what the island looked like at the time, to prove that these witnesses were indeed lying, because if they lie about the conditions in Obonjan, then their entire testimony is brought into question. Why did they strive to present that island as a concentration camp here in the courtroom? At least, this is the way that my small lawyer's mind thinks, and I have to act like a lawyer, as a Defence counsel here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I understand from the print on those pictures, they are taken in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Almost ten years past the period which is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness confirmed that the location looked totally the same at the time where the camp -- where the refugee camp was there. That is what the witness confirmed here in the courtroom, that it looked the same as it does here on these pictures. That's what this witness testified under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I do not believe, Mr. Krsnik, that you're correct about that. I think the witness said that the premises are the same. But you can take any concentration camp, fill it with 20.000 people, take them out, clean it and put 100 people in, and you can't say that it is no longer a concentration camp. It depends on what you do with the same premises afterwards and how many people are there. If you have a dormitory that sleeps six people in normal times and during wartime sleeps 60, then somebody has reason to complain. It has no relevance. The condition of the premises, with happy, healthy language students ten years after the event doesn't help us to understand what the place was like in 1993. You have to see my point, Mr. Krsnik. And I share the view of the President. These photographs are of happy, healthy people, who are not overcrowded and who are not guarded and who are free to come and go. And I think the witness who spoke about the camp, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Clark, first of all, there were no guards. These people went there of their own free will, and the state took care of them. If somebody shut you up in Hotel Intercontinental against your will, you can call it a concentration camp because you are imprisoned or detained there, but if you go there of your own free will, then you cannot call it the concentration camp. This witness did not mention any guards, and he said that everybody was free to come and go as they wanted. My intention was not to show happy, healthy people in this brochure, but what the place looked like. You can see the little bungalows, you can see the swimming pool, you can see the school, and not just happy, healthy people. That was the time when Croatia did all it could to accommodate these refugees, not in camps with guards and not against their will. But if you think it's not relevant, I will now, as always, bow to your will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I honestly feel it has very little relevance to this case and we've probably spent too much time on it but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So as a compromise, we will not admit it into evidence but it has an ID number there. It's just as a reference document in the future, if the issue comes up. Yes, on this point, whether the Prosecution has any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask you to allow me to just reshuffle all my documents, and tomorrow I will present my list of exhibits, if any, I will tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. If I understand the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal correctly, only documents that have been shown to this witness can be admitted, and he was only shown three documents and that's all, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we will apply the same standards in the admitting of the documents for the both parties. Well, the time is up, you understand, and tomorrow morning we will have a new witness. Sorry, tomorrow afternoon, we will have the new witness. I believe that is the witness number 1 in the list you are filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He is going to be heard in public. That's Mr. Milan Kovac. So it will be fully a public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we will rise until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
